source.text: Περὶ δὲ τῶν παρθένων ἐπιταγὴν κυρίου οὐκ ἔχω, γνώμην δὲ δίδωμι ὡς ἠλεημένος ὑπὸ κυρίου πιστὸς εἶναι.

records.literal_gloss: Concerning now the virgins a command of [the] Lord not I have, judgment but I give as having received mercy by [the] Lord trustworthy to be.

en.L: Now concerning the virgins, I do not have a command of [the] Lord, but I give [my] judgment as one who has received mercy from [the] Lord to be trustworthy.
en.B: Now about those who have never married: I have no command from the Lord, but I give my opinion as someone the Lord in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mercy has made trustworthy.
en.R: Now about people who have never married. I do not have a command from the Lord about this. But I will tell you what I think. In {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mercy the Lord has made me someone you can trust.

decisions.choice: virgins: people who have never married, chiefly young women of an age to marry
alternatives: anyone who is sexually inexperienced, whatever their state
decisions.reason: παρθένος named a girl or young woman who had not yet married, and so was presumed a virgin (Matthew 1:23; Luke 1:27). The form here could be masculine or feminine, and the word can be used of men (Revelation 14:4), but in this chapter it is always a woman (7:28, 7:34, 7:36-38). Paul has already spoken to widows and the married (7:8-16); now he turns to those who have never married. In 7:36-38 the word is used of one particular young woman, and its sense there is discussed on 7:36.

decisions.choice: a command of the Lord: a saying of Jesus that settles the question
decisions.reason: In 7:10 Paul could pass on a command of the Lord about divorce (Mark 10:9-12). On the never-married he knows no such saying, so he gives his own judgment (γνώμη), as in 7:12. He does not treat it as worthless: it comes from one the Lord has made trustworthy, and in 7:40 he claims to have the Spirit of God.

decisions.choice: having received mercy to be trustworthy: the Lord's mercy has made Paul reliable
alternatives: having received mercy because he was trustworthy
decisions.reason: The perfect participle ἠλεημένος describes a mercy received in the past whose effect lasts. The infinitive "to be trustworthy" gives the result of that mercy. Paul's reliability is God's gift (1 Timothy 1:12-13), not his own claim to merit. πιστὸς here means "reliable, worthy of trust", as in 4:2.

decisions.choice: those who have never married (B); people who have never married (R)
decisions.reason: "Virgins" puts the stress on sexual experience, while Paul's question is whether such people should marry (m1). Literal keeps "virgins". "Unmarried" is kept for ἄγαμος (7:32, 7:34), which can include the widowed and divorced.

decisions.choice: my opinion (B); what I think (R)
decisions.reason: Paul sets his considered view beside a command of the Lord. "Judgment" today can sound like a verdict on someone; Literal keeps it, and 7:40 uses the same words.

source.text: νομίζω οὖν τοῦτο καλὸν ὑπάρχειν διὰ τὴν ἐνεστῶσαν ἀνάγκην, ὅτι καλὸν ἀνθρώπῳ τὸ οὕτως εἶναι.

records.literal_gloss: I think therefore this good to be because of the present necessity, that [it is] good for a man the so to be.

en.L: I think, then, that this is good because of the present distress: that [it is] good for a {{gender:person|man}} to be so.
en.B: So, because of the crisis we now face, I think this is good: it is good for a {{gender:person|man}} to stay as {{gender:they are|he is}}.
en.R: Because of the hard times we are facing now, I think it is best for you to stay as you are.

decisions.choice: the present distress: a time of pressure and hardship already upon the believers
alternatives: a distress that is about to come
the ordinary constraints of married life
decisions.reason: ἐνεστῶσαν is a perfect participle of a verb meaning "to stand in, to be present" (Romans 8:38; Galatians 1:4, "the present evil age"). ἀνάγκην is constraint or distress (Luke 21:23, of the hardships before the end). Paul does not say what the distress is. It may be a local hardship in Corinth, or the pressures of the last days in general; 7:29-31 links it with the shortness of the time.

decisions.choice: this is good ... that it is good: the second clause spells out what "this" is
alternatives: "because it is good", giving a reason
decisions.reason: ὅτι can mean "that" or "because". Paul starts the sentence, breaks off, and restates his point: what is good is to stay as one is. The repeated καλὸν / καλὸν shows the restart.

decisions.choice: for a person to be so: to stay in one's present state, married or unmarried
alternatives: for a man to stay unmarried
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπῳ is general: anyone. "So" points to staying as one is, the rule of 7:17-24, and 7:27 applies it both ways: the married should not seek release, and the unmarried need not seek a wife.

decisions.choice: {{gender:person|man}} (L, B); {{gender:they are|he is}} (B)
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπῳ means a human being of either sex. Readable says "you", which needs no setting.

decisions.choice: the crisis we now face (B); the hard times we are facing now (R)
decisions.reason: "Distress" and "necessity" are no longer everyday words for a time of pressure. Literal keeps "present distress".

records.literal_gloss: Have you been bound to a wife?

en.L: Have you been bound to a wife?
en.B: Are you bound to a wife?

decisions.choice: bound to a wife: married
decisions.reason: δέδεσαι is the verb Paul uses of the marriage bond in 7:39 and Romans 7:2. The question is addressed to a man ("you" is singular), but the principle applies to everyone (7:28).

decisions.choice: a question that sets up a condition: "Are you married? Then ..."
alternatives: a statement: "You are bound to a wife"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT punctuates it as a question. Either way the sense is conditional: if you are married, do not seek to be free.

decisions.choice: Are you married?
alternatives: Are you bound to a wife?
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the picture of being bound means (m1).

source.text: μὴ ζήτει λύσιν· λέλυσαι ἀπὸ γυναικός;

records.literal_gloss: Not seek release; have you been released from a wife?

en.L: Do not seek release. Have you been released from a wife?
en.B: Do not try to get free. Are you free of a wife?
en.R: Then do not try to end your marriage. Are you single?

decisions.choice: release: ending the marriage by divorce
decisions.reason: λύσιν answers "bound": the release from a marriage is divorce, which Paul has already ruled out for believers in 7:10-13.

decisions.choice: released from a wife: not married now, whether never married, widowed or divorced
decisions.reason: The perfect λέλυσαι could suggest a bond once there and now loosed. But in pairing with "bound" it most likely just means "not tied to a wife", and 7:28 speaks of the unmarried in general.

decisions.choice: try to get free; free of a wife (B); try to end your marriage; single (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the pair "get free / free" for the Greek pair "release / released". Readable says what the release is (m1) and uses an everyday word for being unmarried (m2).

en.B: Do not look for a wife.
en.R: Then do not go looking for a wife.

decisions.choice: do not seek: advice, not a ban
decisions.reason: The same words as "do not seek release" make the two cases match. 7:28 shows this is counsel: marrying is not a sin.

source.text: ἐὰν δὲ καὶ γαμήσῃς, οὐχ ἥμαρτες.

records.literal_gloss: If but also you marry, not you sinned.

en.L: But if indeed you marry, you did not sin.
en.B: Yet if you do marry, you have done nothing sinful.
en.R: But if you get married, that is not a sin.

decisions.choice: if you marry, you have not sinned: marrying is no sin
decisions.reason: The aorist ἥμαρτες after a condition about the future looks at the act as complete: should you marry, the deed would not be a sin. Paul guards against anyone who took his advice as a rule (7:1, 7:36).

decisions.choice: you have done nothing sinful (B); that is not a sin (R)
decisions.reason: Says that the act itself is not sinful, which is the point of the aorist (m1).

source.text: καὶ ἐὰν γήμῃ ἡ παρθένος, οὐχ ἥμαρτεν.

records.literal_gloss: And if marries the virgin, not she sinned.

en.L: And if the virgin marries, she did not sin.
en.B: And if a young woman who has never married takes a husband, she has done nothing sinful.
en.R: And if a young woman who has never married gets married, that is not a sin.

decisions.choice: the virgin: any young woman who has not yet married
decisions.reason: The article is generic: the class of such women, as in 7:25.

decisions.choice: a young woman who has never married
decisions.reason: As in 7:25 (r-en-1), the English names her state in life rather than her sexual experience.

source.text: θλῖψιν δὲ τῇ σαρκὶ ἕξουσιν οἱ τοιοῦτοι, ἐγὼ δὲ ὑμῶν φείδομαι.

records.literal_gloss: Affliction but in the flesh will have the such, I but you am sparing.

en.L: But such [people] will have affliction in the flesh, and I am sparing you.
en.B: But such people will meet hardship in this earthly life, and I am trying to spare you.
en.R: But married people will have troubles in their everyday lives, and I want to keep you from them.

decisions.choice: in the flesh: in ordinary bodily, earthly life
decisions.reason: σάρξ here is not the sinful human outlook of 3:1-3 but bodily life in this world (2 Corinthians 4:11; Galatians 2:20). Those who marry will face the pressures that come with a household, all the more in "the present distress" (7:26).

decisions.choice: affliction: pressure and hardship
decisions.reason: θλῖψις is a general word for pressure and trouble. Here it is the hardship of married life in hard times, not persecution as such.

decisions.choice: I am sparing you: I want to spare you, by this advice
alternatives: I will not say more, to spare you
decisions.reason: The present φείδομαι describes what Paul is trying to do in giving this counsel.

decisions.choice: hardship in this earthly life (B); troubles in their everyday lives (R)
decisions.reason: Follows the book-wide choices for θλῖψις (affliction, hardship, trouble). "In the flesh" is said plainly (m1), since in English it suggests sinful nature.

decisions.choice: married people
decisions.reason: Readable says who "such people" are: those who marry, the subject of the two sentences before.

source.text: τοῦτο δέ φημι, ἀδελφοί, ὁ καιρὸς συνεσταλμένος ἐστίν· τὸ λοιπὸν ἵνα καὶ οἱ ἔχοντες γυναῖκας ὡς μὴ ἔχοντες ὦσιν, καὶ οἱ κλαίοντες ὡς μὴ κλαίοντες, καὶ οἱ χαίροντες ὡς μὴ χαίροντες, καὶ οἱ ἀγοράζοντες ὡς μὴ κατέχοντες, καὶ οἱ χρώμενοι τὸν κόσμον ὡς μὴ καταχρώμενοι· παράγει γὰρ τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ κόσμου τούτου.

records.literal_gloss: This now I say, brothers, the time shortened is; the remaining that both those having wives as not having be, \v 30 and those weeping as not weeping, and those rejoicing as not rejoicing, and those buying as not possessing, \v 31 and those using the world as not using fully; is passing away for the form of the world this.

en.L: But this I say, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}: the time has been shortened. From now on, [let] both those having wives be as not having, \v 30 and those weeping as not weeping, and those rejoicing as not rejoicing, and those buying as not possessing, \v 31 and those using the world as not using [it] to the full; for the form of this world is passing away.
en.B: Here is my point, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}: the time has been cut short. So from now on, married men should be as though they had no wives, \v 30 those who weep as though they did not weep, those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, those who buy as though they kept nothing, \v 31 and those who deal with the world as though they did not use it to the full. For this world's present shape is passing away.
en.R: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, this is what I mean. There is not much time left. From now on, married men should live as if they had no wives. \v 30 People who are sad should live as if they were not sad. People who are happy should live as if they were not happy. People who buy things should live as if those things were not really theirs. \v 31 People who use what this world offers should not get wrapped up in it. For this world, as it is now, is passing away.

decisions.choice: the time has been shortened: the time until the end has been drawn in, so that little remains
decisions.reason: συνεσταλμένος means drawn together or compressed. καιρός is the time God has set (Romans 13:11). Since Christ came, the present age is running out (10:11, "the ends of the ages"), and this shapes how believers hold everything in it. Paul does not name a date.

decisions.choice: from now on ... should: a call for how believers are to live
alternatives: "so that": the purpose for which God shortened the time
"the time that remains is short", joining these words to what comes before
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT places a raised dot before τὸ λοιπὸν, so these words begin the new clause. The clause with ἵνα can state God's purpose or give an instruction; either way it describes how believers are to live now.

decisions.choice: as not: living in each state without being ruled by it
alternatives: giving up marriage, grief, joy and possessions
decisions.reason: Paul does not tell husbands to leave their wives (7:10-13) or forbid weeping and rejoicing (Romans 12:15). Each "as not" means holding these things loosely, because none of them is lasting.

decisions.choice: the world: the present order of human life, with its goods, dealings and ways, which is passing
decisions.reason: κόσμος here is the world of everyday affairs that believers use and deal with: buying, owning and the like. It is not evil in itself, but it is not permanent. καταχρώμενοι means to use fully or use up; the believer uses the world without being consumed by it. σχῆμα is outward form or way of being (Philippians 2:8): the world as it now is passes away (1 John 2:17).

decisions.choice: cut short (B); there is not much time left (R)
decisions.reason: "Cut short" keeps the sense that the time has been shortened (m1); Readable says what that means for the hearers.

decisions.choice: this world's present shape (B); this world, as it is now (R)
decisions.reason: "Form" can suggest a document or a shape on paper; the point is the way the world now is (m4). Literal keeps "form".

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: The address includes the whole church, women as well as men, as the book-wide choice for ἀδελφός has it.

records.literal_gloss: I want but you free from care to be.

en.L: But I want you to be free from cares.
en.B: I want you to be free from cares that divide you.
en.R: I want you to be free from worry.

decisions.choice: free from care: not pulled two ways by competing concerns
decisions.reason: ἀμερίμνους begins a play on the verb in the next sentences: the unmarried "care for" the things of the Lord, the married also for the things of the world. Paul does not mean that the unmarried have no concerns, but that their concern is undivided (7:33-35).

decisions.choice: free from cares that divide you
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the word "care" that the next sentences repeat, and says what kind of care is meant (m1), so that the unmarried man's "care" for the Lord does not seem to contradict this wish.

source.text: ὁ ἄγαμος μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κυρίου, πῶς ἀρέσῃ τῷ κυρίῳ·

records.literal_gloss: The unmarried cares for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord;

en.L: The unmarried [man] cares for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord.
en.B: The unmarried man gives his care to the things of the Lord, how he may please {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
en.R: A man without a wife thinks about the things of the Lord and how to please {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: cares for the things of the Lord: gives his attention to the Lord's work and service
decisions.reason: μεριμνᾷ here is a good kind of care, as in 12:25 and Philippians 2:20. "The things of the Lord" are what concerns him: his service and his people.

decisions.choice: the unmarried man: any man without a wife
alternatives: a man who has never married
decisions.reason: ἄγαμος is broader than "virgin": in 7:8 and 7:11 it includes the widowed and the separated.

decisions.choice: gives his care to
decisions.reason: Keeps the word "care" from 7:32a and avoids "anxious", which would make his care for the Lord sound like a fault.

source.text: ὁ δὲ γαμήσας μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κόσμου, πῶς ἀρέσῃ τῇ γυναικί, καὶ μεμέρισται.

records.literal_gloss: The but having married cares for the things of the world, how he may please the wife, \v 34 and he is divided.

en.L: But the [one] who married cares for the things of the world, how he may please the wife, \v 34 and he is divided.
en.B: But the married man gives his care to the things of the world, how he may please his wife, \v 34 and he is pulled two ways.
en.R: But a married man has to think about the things of this world and how to please his wife. \v 34 So he is pulled in two directions.

decisions.choice: the things of the world: the everyday affairs of this life, such as a household and its needs
decisions.reason: κόσμος here is the world of 7:31: the order of ordinary life, which is passing. Pleasing one's wife is not sin; Paul has said husband and wife owe each other care (7:3-5). The point is that a married man's attention is shared.

decisions.choice: he is divided: his attention is split between the Lord and his wife
alternatives: "the wife and the virgin are also divided (different)", joining the verb to the next words
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT ends the sentence after μεμέρισται, so the verb completes the description of the married man. Some manuscripts join it to what follows; see the note on the next sentence.

decisions.choice: pulled two ways (B); pulled in two directions (R)
decisions.reason: "Divided" alone can suggest a split mind or a broken loyalty; the picture is of attention drawn two ways (m2).

source.text: καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄγαμος καὶ ἡ παρθένος μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κυρίου, ἵνα ᾖ ἁγία καὶ τῷ σώματι καὶ τῷ πνεύματι· ἡ δὲ γαμήσασα μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κόσμου, πῶς ἀρέσῃ τῷ ἀνδρί.

records.literal_gloss: And the woman the unmarried and the virgin cares for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in the body and in the spirit; the but having married cares for the things of the world, how she may please the husband.

en.L: And the unmarried woman and the virgin care for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in the body and in the spirit; but the [woman] who married cares for the things of the world, how she may please the husband.
en.B: And the unmarried woman, or the young woman who has never married, gives her care to the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body as well as in spirit. But the married woman gives her care to the things of the world, how she may please her husband.
en.R: A woman who is not married, whether she was married before or has never married, thinks about the things of the Lord. She wants to be set apart for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in body and in spirit. But a married woman has to think about the things of this world and how to please her husband.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "he is divided. And the unmarried woman and the virgin care for ..."
alternatives: "There is a difference between the wife and the virgin. The unmarried woman cares for ..."
"the unmarried woman and the unmarried virgin"
decisions.reason: The manuscripts differ here in several ways. The reading behind the King James Version joins μεμέρισται to the women ("the wife and the virgin are different") and has "the unmarried woman" begin the next clause. Other manuscripts place "unmarried" after "virgin" as well. The SBLGNT reading gives the clearest parallel to the unmarried and married man. Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the unmarried woman and the virgin: a woman without a husband now (widowed or separated), and a young woman who has never married
alternatives: two names for the same woman
decisions.reason: ἄγαμος covers anyone without a spouse (7:8, 7:11), while παρθένος is the never-married woman of 7:25 and 7:28. Paul names both so that every woman without a husband is included. The singular verb treats them as one group.

decisions.choice: holy in body and spirit: wholly set apart for the Lord
decisions.reason: ἅγιος means set apart for God. "Body and spirit" means the whole person (2 Corinthians 7:1). Paul does not say married women are unholy; he has just called the believing household holy (7:14). The point is undivided devotion.

decisions.choice: whether she was married before or has never married; set apart for him
alternatives: the unmarried woman and the virgin; holy
decisions.reason: Readable says why Paul names two kinds of women (m2), and what "holy" means here (m3).

source.text: τοῦτο δὲ πρὸς τὸ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν σύμφορον λέγω, οὐχ ἵνα βρόχον ὑμῖν ἐπιβάλω, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸ εὔσχημον καὶ εὐπάρεδρον τῷ κυρίῳ ἀπερισπάστως.

records.literal_gloss: This now for the of you yourselves benefit I say, not that a noose on you I may throw, but for the seemly and devoted to the Lord undistractedly.

en.L: Now I say this for your own benefit, not that I may throw a noose on you, but for what is seemly and devoted to the Lord without distraction.
en.B: I tell you this to help you, not to throw a noose over you. I want you to live as is fitting and to stay close beside the Lord with nothing to draw you away.
en.R: I am telling you this to help you, not to tie you down. I want you to live in a good and proper way and to give yourselves to the Lord without anything pulling you away.

decisions.choice: throw a noose on you: put a restraint on you, as one would catch an animal
decisions.reason: βρόχος is a noose or snare used in hunting or for restraining. Paul's advice is not meant to tie them down; marriage remains free (7:28, 7:36).

decisions.choice: what is fitting and devoted to the Lord: a life that is seemly and constantly at the Lord's service
decisions.reason: εὐσχήμων means proper or becoming. εὐπάρεδρον means sitting constantly beside someone, like an attendant waiting on a master. ἀπερισπάστως answers the "divided" man of 7:33-34: nothing drags such a person away.

decisions.choice: stay close beside the Lord with nothing to draw you away (B); give yourselves to the Lord without anything pulling you away (R)
alternatives: devotion to the Lord without distraction
decisions.reason: Keeps the picture of sitting beside the Lord (m2), and says "without distraction" in plainer words.

decisions.choice: tie you down
decisions.reason: Readable uses an everyday idiom with the same sense (m1).

source.text: Εἰ δέ τις ἀσχημονεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν παρθένον αὐτοῦ νομίζει ἐὰν ᾖ ὑπέρακμος, καὶ οὕτως ὀφείλει γίνεσθαι, ὃ θέλει ποιείτω· οὐχ ἁμαρτάνει· γαμείτωσαν.

records.literal_gloss: If but anyone to behave improperly toward the virgin of him thinks, if he be beyond-the-peak, and so it ought to be, what he wishes let him do; not he sins; let them marry.

en.L: But if anyone thinks he is behaving improperly toward his virgin, if he is past [the] peak, and so it ought to happen, let him do what he wishes; he does not sin; let them marry.
en.B: Now if a man thinks he is not treating the woman he is engaged to rightly, because his desire for her is strong and the marriage ought to go ahead, he may do what he wants. He commits no sin. Let the two of them marry.
en.R: Suppose a man is engaged to a young woman, and he thinks he is not being fair to her. Maybe his desire for her is too strong, and he feels they should marry. Then he should do what he wants. It is not a sin for the two of them to marry.

decisions.choice: his virgin: the young woman a man is engaged to marry
alternatives: his unmarried daughter, whom a father may give in marriage
a woman living with him in a marriage without sexual relations
decisions.reason: The passage can be read in two main ways. (1) A man and the woman he is engaged to: he wonders whether he is treating her rightly by holding back from marriage, and Paul says they may marry; if he is settled in mind, keeping her as she is, unmarried, is also right. (2) A father, or guardian, and his unmarried daughter: he wonders whether he is wronging her by not giving her in marriage, and Paul says he may let the couple marry. The strongest point for (2) is that γαμίζω in 7:38 elsewhere means "give in marriage" (Mark 12:25; Luke 17:27). For (1): the man's own desire and will are stressed (7:37), "his virgin" is an odd way to name a daughter, and "let them marry" most naturally means the man and the woman. A third view, that the two lived together in a celibate marriage, has little support in the text. This translation takes (1), at every level.

decisions.choice: beyond the peak: his desire is strong, at full strength or more
alternatives: she is past the usual age for marriage
decisions.reason: ὑπέρακμος means "beyond the peak". The form can refer to a man or a woman, and the subject of ᾖ is not stated. Said of the man, it means that his passion is at its height or overflowing, which fits 7:9 and the contrast in 7:37, where the man has his desire under control. Said of the woman, it means she is past the bloom of youth, which would fit the father reading.

decisions.choice: behave improperly toward her: treat her in a way that is not right or honorable
decisions.reason: ἀσχημονέω means to act in an unseemly or shameful way (13:5). It may mean keeping her waiting without marriage, or the risk of sexual sin under strong desire (7:2, 7:9). Either way, marrying ends the problem.

decisions.choice: and so it ought to be ... let them marry: if marriage is the right course, the couple should marry
decisions.reason: "So it ought to be" refers to marriage as the fitting outcome. The plural γαμείτωσαν brings in both of them: the man and the woman marry each other.

decisions.choice: the woman he is engaged to (B); a young woman he is engaged to (R)
decisions.reason: Says plainly whom "his virgin" means on the reading taken (m1). Literal keeps "his virgin", which leaves the other reading open. "Betrothed" is no longer everyday English.

decisions.choice: his desire for her is strong (B); his desire for her is too strong (R)
alternatives: if he is past the peak
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "past the peak" means on the reading taken (m2).

source.text: ὃς δὲ ἕστηκεν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ ἑδραῖος μὴ ἔχων ἀνάγκην, ἐξουσίαν δὲ ἔχει περὶ τοῦ ἰδίου θελήματος, καὶ τοῦτο κέκρικεν ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ καρδίᾳ, τηρεῖν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ παρθένον, καλῶς ποιήσει·

records.literal_gloss: Who but stands in the heart of him firm, not having necessity, authority but has concerning the own will, and this has decided in the own heart, to keep the of himself virgin, well he will do;

en.L: But [he] who stands firm in his heart, not having necessity, but has authority over his own will, and has decided this in his own heart, to keep his own virgin, will do well.
en.B: But suppose a man stands firm in his heart. He is under no pressure, he has control over his own will, and he has decided in his own heart that the woman he is engaged to should stay as she is. He will do well.
en.R: But another man may have made up his mind firmly. He does not feel he must marry, and he is in control of what he wants. He has decided in his heart not to marry the young woman. That man will be doing what is right.

decisions.choice: under no necessity, with authority over his own will: not driven by desire, and free to decide
decisions.reason: ἀνάγκη is the same word as in 7:26, here an inner pressure: the strong desire of 7:36. Having ἐξουσία over his will means he is master of his desires (7:9). On the father reading, it would mean no outside pressure prevents him from deciding.

decisions.choice: to keep his virgin: to keep her as she is, that is, not to marry her
alternatives: to keep his daughter at home unmarried
decisions.reason: τηρεῖν means to keep or preserve. On the reading taken at 7:36 (m1 there), the man chooses not to marry. On the father reading, he keeps his daughter unmarried.

decisions.choice: that the woman he is engaged to should stay as she is
alternatives: to keep her as his betrothed
decisions.reason: Balanced follows the reading taken at 7:36 and says what keeping her means without going beyond the Greek. Readable says it plainly: "not to marry the young woman".

decisions.choice: He does not feel he must marry
decisions.reason: Readable says what the pressure is (m1).

source.text: ὥστε καὶ ὁ γαμίζων τὴν παρθένον ἑαυτοῦ καλῶς ποιεῖ, καὶ ὁ μὴ γαμίζων κρεῖσσον ποιήσει.

records.literal_gloss: So that both the marrying the virgin of himself well does, and the not marrying better will do.

en.L: So then, both the [one] marrying his own virgin does well, and the [one] not marrying will do better.
en.B: So the man who marries the woman he is engaged to does well, and the man who does not marry her will do better.
en.R: So a man who marries the young woman he is engaged to is doing a good thing. And a man who does not marry will be doing something even better.

decisions.choice: marrying: taking her as his wife
alternatives: giving her in marriage, as a father gives his daughter
decisions.reason: Elsewhere in the New Testament γαμίζω means "give in marriage" (Mark 12:25; Luke 17:27), and that is the main support for the father reading of 7:36-38. On the reading taken at 7:36 (m1 there), Paul uses it here for the man who marries. The choice follows that decision.

decisions.choice: well ... better: both choices are good; not marrying is better in view of the present time
decisions.reason: Paul has given his reasons in 7:26-35: the present distress, the shortness of the time and undivided devotion to the Lord. He has also said marriage is no sin (7:28, 7:36) and that each person has his own gift (7:7).

source.text: Γυνὴ δέδεται ἐφ’ ὅσον χρόνον ζῇ ὁ ἀνὴρ αὐτῆς· ἐὰν δὲ κοιμηθῇ ὁ ἀνήρ, ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶν ᾧ θέλει γαμηθῆναι, μόνον ἐν κυρίῳ·

records.literal_gloss: A wife is bound for as much time as lives the husband of her; if but falls asleep the husband, free she is to whom she wishes to be married, only in [the] Lord;

en.L: A wife is bound for as long a time as her husband lives; but if the husband falls asleep, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in [the] Lord.
en.B: A wife remains bound for as long as her husband is living. Should her husband die, she is free to marry whomever she wants, though only a man who belongs to the Lord.
en.R: A wife is joined to her husband for as long as he is alive. But if he dies, she may marry anyone she wants, as long as he is a follower of the Lord.

decisions.choice: falls asleep: dies
decisions.reason: κοιμάομαι is a common way of speaking of the death of believers (11:30; 15:6, 15:18; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-15).

decisions.choice: only in the Lord: she must marry a fellow believer
alternatives: she must marry in a Christian way, whoever the husband is
decisions.reason: "In the Lord" describes one who belongs to Christ (Romans 16:8-13). The limit most naturally applies to the man she marries. Paul allowed believers already married to unbelievers to stay married (7:12-14); this is about entering a new marriage (2 Corinthians 6:14).

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "a wife is bound"
decisions.reason: Some later manuscripts add "by law", probably from Romans 7:2. The sense is not changed. Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: dies
decisions.reason: The idiom (m1) is said plainly; Literal keeps it.

decisions.choice: only a man who belongs to the Lord (B); as long as he is a follower of the Lord (R)
decisions.reason: Says what "in the Lord" means here (m2).

source.text: μακαριωτέρα δέ ἐστιν ἐὰν οὕτως μείνῃ, κατὰ τὴν ἐμὴν γνώμην, δοκῶ δὲ κἀγὼ πνεῦμα θεοῦ ἔχειν.

records.literal_gloss: More blessed but she is if so she remains, according to the my judgment; I think but I also [the] Spirit of God to have.

en.L: But she is more blessed if she remains so, according to my judgment; and I think that I also have [the] Spirit of God.
en.B: Even so, in my opinion she is more blessed if she remains a widow. And I believe that I too have the Spirit of God.
en.R: But I think she will be better off if she does not marry again. And I believe God's Spirit is guiding me too.

decisions.choice: more blessed: better off, in the fuller sense of a life given to the Lord without distraction
decisions.reason: μακάριος is the word of the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-11). Paul's reasons for preferring that she stay unmarried are those of 7:26-35, not merely her contentment.

decisions.choice: I think that I too have the Spirit of God: a modest but firm claim to the Spirit's guidance
alternatives: real uncertainty about whether he has the Spirit
decisions.reason: δοκῶ is restrained, perhaps with irony, and κἀγὼ ("I too") suggests that some in Corinth claimed the Spirit for their own views (14:37). Paul's opinion is not a command of the Lord (7:25), but it is given by one led by God's Spirit (2:12-16).

decisions.choice: if she remains a widow (B); if she does not marry again (R)
decisions.reason: Says what "so" refers to: the widow of 7:39 staying unmarried.

decisions.choice: God's Spirit is guiding me too
alternatives: I too have the Spirit of God
decisions.reason: Readable says what having the Spirit means for Paul's advice (m2).
